title: Worked Example: Quadratic Naive List Reversal
body_html:
Worked Example: Quadratic Naive List Reversal

The append-at-the-end naive list reversal, instrumented in CostM ℕ to exhibit a quadratic cost. Each of the length recursive steps performs an append whose cost is proportional to the accumulated length, giving $$ (\operatorname{naiveReverse}\,l).\mathrm{cost} \;\le\; |l|^2, $$ proved as naiveReverse_cost_le. This is the counterpoint to the linear and logarithmic CostM ℕ examples (Worked Example: Euclidean GCD Step Count): a worse algorithm shows up directly as a worse bound on .cost, with no change to the monad or to the correctness of the reversed result on .ret.

Lean declarations

  • ReverseSpace.naiveReverse : List α → CostM ℕ (List α).
  • ReverseSpace.naiveReverse_cost_le — the |l|² cost bound.

References

  • [Danielsson 2008] Nils Anders Danielsson, POPL 2008. Cost-annotated functional algorithms (The CostM Complexity Monad).

lean_refs.name: ReverseSpace.naiveReverse
lean_refs.signature:
def naiveReverse {A : Type} : List A → CostM ℕ (List A)
  | []      => pure []
  | a :: as => do
    ✓[as.length + 1] do
      let rest ← naiveReverse as
      pure (rest ++ [a])
/-- Cumulative `++` allocation is quadratic in input length. -/

lean_refs.name: ReverseSpace.naiveReverse_cost_le
lean_refs.signature:
theorem naiveReverse_cost_le {A : Type} (l : List A) :
    (naiveReverse l).cost ≤ l.length * l.length
lean_refs.docstring: Cumulative `++` allocation is quadratic in input length.
